commenti.body: Y’all seen Barry Lyndon? Just watched it today. Shit’s fire

I haven’t watched a lot of classics for the past year, cause I’ve been in the mood for contemporary film. But for Thanksgiving I’m planning on playing a few classics I’ve never seen. Y’all got any recommendations? I would love some films from the 40s and 50s, and I don’t care what country or language. Maybe some stuff that’s not as talked-about, since I have checked out a lot of the “canonical” directors (Renoir, Welles, Bergman, Fellini, Kurosawa, Ozu, etc., etc.).

Not the most obscure but a few of my favourites from around that time would be 

Make Way For Tomorrow 

The Ox Bow Incident 

To Be Or Not To Be 

Night And The City 

Le Trou 

Seven Men From Now
Looks like a set of excellent recommendations!  I’ve never heard of any of them.  Thank you!
Do you have the Criterion Channel?

If you’re into slightly lesser known animation, I highly recommend Karel Zeman. I know that at least three of his feature films are on Criterion Channel— *Journey to the Beginning of Time*, *Invention for Destruction*, and *The Fabulous Baron Munchausen*, as well as several of his shorts. They’re from the late 50’s, so it just barely fits the parameters of what you’re looking for, but I always love name dropping them whenever I get the chance.

Powell & Pressburger retrospective, specifically the films from 1943 to 1948.

Apu trilogy

Preston Sturges

John Huston

*Great Expectations*

*Brief Encounter*

*La Belle et la Bête*

*Les Enfants du Paradis*

*Gaslight*

*Gojira*

I just watched *The Earrings of Madame De....* (Max Ophuls 1953) and it's not an exaggeration to say it blew me away a little bit. I was not prepared for a film from the early 50s to feel this tense and contemporary. And edgy and slick, and also funny. It thrilled me is the truth. 

Also French but from 1945 is *Les Enfants Du Paradis* by Marcel Carne. It's a total classic so you may have seen it, but anyway it's tremendous. It's also one of those fascinating films produced under occupation. Maybe an interesting companion piece to *Opfergang* (1944 Viet Harlan), a opulent German romance made amid the ruins of war, and a mind-bindingly intense fever dream to boot. Amazing. 

But my personal favourite film from this period is *Francesco, giullare di Dio* which is by a canonical director (sorry) but maybe it's one not many people talk about much. The director is Rossellini and the film is from 1950. It's a collection of short stories from the life of St Francis. Some are sad, some funny, some like parables, but all are enchanting as hell. The passage where St Francis meets the leper is surely one of the most beautiful in cinema. Prepare for odd little monks running over fields like herds of cattle. (The monks, including St Francis himself, were all played by actual Franciscan monks). (Funny trivia story from IMBD - Rossellini wanted to thank the monks for participating in the film, so asked what he could give them as a gift. Everyone expected they would ask for a donation to charity, but they asked for a fireworks display. Monks, eh?)

Kiss Me Deadly (1955) is a great noir film that prefigures - and go with me here - Gremlins 2, in that the director thought his source material was ridiculous and really went crazy with it. In the case the source material is a Mike Hammer novel instead of, uh, Gremlins, but nevertheless an excellent film.

If anyone is interested in a critical look at the film It's A Wonderful Life there's a new 10 part podcast on iHeart that examines it's cultural significance. It covers everything from examining if Mary Hatch was the real hero to the idea that everywhere in the US has become Pottersville to why Ayn Rand felt the film was a threat to the the capitalist system and had the FBI investigate it. 
https://www.iheart.com/podcast/1119-george-bailey-was-never-b-127106279/

I watched “Madame De…” a couple years ago and recall it to be shocking and touching.  That ending is amazing.

Probably going to watch “Children of Paradise,” as you suggest.  It’s been on my list to-watch for ages, and I remember some stills from the film that look striking.

What are people’s thoughts on Saltburn? I enjoyed it, I think it lost a bit of momentum towards the end and definitely should have scrapped the monologue - but Keoghan’s acting rescued it a lot for me and the final scene was great.

I do think that it’s a bit of a different experience watching it when you’re British and understand some of the subtleties regarding the class system here and how that bleeds into the themes of the film. But I can see how it would be divisive nonetheless.

Why the fuck does everyone talk in movies now? The past three films I've seen in theaters have all had people near me talking loudly during at least half the runtime. It's obnoxious, why pay to see a movie in a theater and then talk?
